cases.purpose: Three scripts queued by one shell with batch are accepted by separate cron run --once polls with a fixed clock, executed once each and removed; a second poll executes nothing.
cases.oracle: Documented bash-os contract (batch_doc and cron_doc): batch reads a script from stdin and queues ${BASHCRON_SPOOL_DIR}/atjobs/<seconds>.<pid>.<seq>.job whose first line is "# run_at=<seconds>"; cron's scanner runs ready jobs in submission (FIFO) order and removes them; "low load" is currently immediate. Expectations are computed by the observer from facts it controls (submitter pids, wall-clock seconds, the order in which it released each submitter, the fixed consumer clock), never from candidate output.
cases.comparison: Producer and consumer are separate candidate shells over one private spool (BASHCRON_SPOOL_DIR, OUTPUT, ETC and CROND under /tmp/parity-case/work/batch-once). Compared: the three "job <id> scheduled for <sec>" lines (id shape, seconds, submitter pid), the queued files (0600, exact bytes: "# run_at=<sec>" header plus the script), the labels executed by poll 1 (each exactly once), an empty atjobs directory afterwards (no .job and no .running leftover), and an unchanged job log after poll 2. Every observation is in observations.jsonl; tables, clock and state files, job logs, spool listings and daemon streams stay in the case workspace, which the harness preserves.

cases.purpose: Jobs queued in the same second by two different shells run in submission order whichever shell has the lower pid; submitted one second apart the order is also submission order (control).
cases.oracle: Documented bash-os contract (batch_doc and cron_doc): batch reads a script from stdin and queues ${BASHCRON_SPOOL_DIR}/atjobs/<seconds>.<pid>.<seq>.job whose first line is "# run_at=<seconds>"; cron's scanner runs ready jobs in submission (FIFO) order and removes them; "low load" is currently immediate. Expectations are computed by the observer from facts it controls (submitter pids, wall-clock seconds, the order in which it released each submitter, the fixed consumer clock), never from candidate output. Source note: ids sort by strcmp over <sec>.<pid>.<seq>, so within one second the pid text, not submission order, decides (batch.c:116-119, cron.c:865-892).
cases.comparison: Two candidate shells are spawned (the first has the lower pid) and each blocks until the observer releases it. The observer releases them in the stated order inside one aligned second (retried until both ids carry the same second), runs one consumer poll with a fixed clock, and compares the execution order with the release order. The last row releases the higher-pid shell first and the lower-pid shell in the following second. Ids, pids, seconds and the log are retained. Every observation is in observations.jsonl; tables, clock and state files, job logs, spool listings and daemon streams stay in the case workspace, which the harness preserves.

cases.purpose: cron run keeps polling at --interval and dispatches the due entry of each new minute once, without re-dispatching a minute on later polls.
cases.oracle: Documented bash-os contract (cron_doc): cron run polls the spool, system crontab, cron.d and per-user tables; each poll consumes one BASHCRON_NOW_FILE line and EOF reuses the last; @reboot runs once when daemon mode starts and is not run by --once; BASHCRON_CATCHUP_MAX_MIN (1..1440, default 5) bounds minute-by-minute replay after a forward gap and larger gaps collapse to the current minute; BASHCRON_STATE_FILE persists the last evaluated minute floor(epoch/60) with mode 0600. Expected marker sequences are derived by hand from those rules and calendar arithmetic (base 2023-11-14 12:10:00 UTC, offset k is minute 10+k), independent of the candidate.
cases.comparison: An owned daemon child runs `cron run --interval 2` over a private per-user table (rows for offsets 0, 1, 2), the clock read from BASHCRON_NOW_FILE (12:10:10, 12:11:25, 12:12:40) and no state file. Compared: the rows dispatched at successive polls (P0,P1,P2 in order, once each); two later polls with the clock exhausted, proven by two heartbeat at-jobs each executed by a later poll, adding no duplicate; and the gap between consecutive observed executions (at least 1.75 s for the 2 s interval). Every observation is in observations.jsonl; tables, clock and state files, job logs, spool listings and daemon streams stay in the case workspace, which the harness preserves. Each daemon owns a session: after the last observation the observer SIGKILLs anything left in it, waits until none of it is alive, reaps the leader and records the outcome (kind=daemon-finish), so the harness finds no live child; the setup controls use stand-ins that start no external process and verify the same teardown.

cases.purpose: SIGHUP makes the daemon re-read its tables and evaluate immediately (repeatedly), a table change is not picked up without it, and SIGTERM stops it promptly with status 0 and no leftovers.
cases.oracle: Documented bash-os contract (cron_doc): cron run polls the spool, system crontab, cron.d and per-user tables; each poll consumes one BASHCRON_NOW_FILE line and EOF reuses the last; @reboot runs once when daemon mode starts and is not run by --once; BASHCRON_CATCHUP_MAX_MIN (1..1440, default 5) bounds minute-by-minute replay after a forward gap and larger gaps collapse to the current minute; BASHCRON_STATE_FILE persists the last evaluated minute floor(epoch/60) with mode 0600. Expected marker sequences are derived by hand from those rules and calendar arithmetic (base 2023-11-14 12:10:00 UTC, offset k is minute 10+k), independent of the candidate. SIGHUP and SIGTERM behavior is not described in cron_doc; the obligation (cron/deferred-daemon-lifecycle r4) and the handlers in cron.c:1649-1651 define it.
cases.comparison: An owned daemon child runs with a 3600 s interval and a fixed clock, so no regular poll can occur; a state file replaced by every saving poll is the completion signal. Compared: the first dispatch, a negative control (table rewritten, no signal, nothing runs and no poll saves), two SIGHUP reloads each running only the new row while the daemon stays alive, and SIGTERM (exit status 0 within 3 s, no job.* captures or .running files left, state file intact with mode 0600). Signals go only to the owned child, after its first poll. Every observation is in observations.jsonl; tables, clock and state files, job logs, spool listings and daemon streams stay in the case workspace, which the harness preserves. Each daemon owns a session: after the last observation the observer SIGKILLs anything left in it, waits until none of it is alive, reaps the leader and records the outcome (kind=daemon-finish), so the harness finds no live child; the setup controls use stand-ins that start no external process and verify the same teardown.

sighup-1: ran=A,B alive=yes
